newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Smugglers profit on India-Bangladesh border.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Smugglers profit on India-Bangladesh border.

text.p: Bangladesh and its giant neighbour India exchange goods worth $2 billion a year in official trade, but how much they transact unofficially is anybody's guess.
Loadbearers from 10-year-old boys to wooden carts powered by oxen are busy carrying commodities smuggled from India.
It is a common scene virtually everywhere in Chapainawabganj district in northwestern Bangladesh and in all other districts bordering India.
"Smuggling is our main source of living," said a young porter, weighed down by a heavy load of Indian mangoes.
No one involved in smuggling would give his or her real name.
"Sit quiet and just watch," said a Chapainawabganj reporter to Reuters correspondents at a remote village a stone's throw from India.

Under a sprawling bamboo grove in that village, dozens of men, women and children were processing, weighing and packaging India's succulent "Fazli" and "Lengra" mango varieties for shipment to Dhaka and elsewhere in Bangladesh.
"What you see is just a drop in the sea," said a village headman.
Goods that trickle in range from toothpaste to cattle -- all under the noses of police.
"Everyone gets a share of it," said smuggler Rasul Mollah, smiling.
"There is no check on the border, but later we have to cross many checkpoints inside the country. At every stop we need to pay something in cash or kind," he said.
BANGLADESH GROWING AS MARKET FOR INDIAN GOODS
India's exports to Bangladesh, growing at an annual rate of 20 to 25 percent, reached $1.2 billion in 1995/96 while its imports from Bangladesh were $70 million.
But trading sources claim another $2 billion or more worth of Indian goods are smuggled into Bangladesh a year, making the country India's fifth largest export source.
Three years ago Bangladesh introduced a tax for importing cattle from India, but hardly 20 percent of some 200,000 head of cattle brought in every month are actually taxed, traders said.

Officials and non-government organisations working in Chapainawabganj and neighbouring Rajshahi district said at least 70 percent of the region's population were directly or indirectly involved in smuggling.
"It's a means to overcome unemployment and poverty. Some people who are not poor also get into the business (of smuggling) to become more rich, in a short-cut way," Mollah said.
"The battle for survival is very tough here," said a local council official. "Only a few people own most of the land and they cheat others who sell their labour," he added.
INDIA OFFERS CHEAPER GOODS
Indian goods are much cheaper. A kilogram of Indian sugar sells for 25 taka in Chapainawabganj against 35 or 40 taka for locally produced sugar.
A new Indian bicycle is available for 1,200 taka, three times cheaper than a Bangladeshi bicycle.
At weekly markets along the borders, sellers from the other side step in without passport or visa.
Bangladeshis also visit India frequently without travel documents.
SMUGGLING IS A FREE-FOR-ALL TRADE
Items smuggled from Bangladesh are few but costly. They include jewellery, electronics, and foreign-made cosmetics and cigarettes.
Drugs available from India include cocaine, heroin and Phensidyl, a cough syrup made with codeine phosphate, which anti-narcotics officials say is now most widely used in Bangladesh.
Bangladesh banned production of cough syrup with codeine phosphate, a substance derived from cocaine, in 1982.
In the village of Tappu, overlooking India's Telkupi village, smugglers ferried goods on their heads or in bullock-carts in broad daylight. Women gave them a helping hand.
A police officer in Chapainawabganj blamed the spate of smuggling on grinding poverty along the frontiers and the apathy of successive governments to help them.
